title: CASE OF BYSTRÝ v. SLOVAKIA
conclusion: Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment;Inhuman treatment) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect)
summary: In Bystrý v. Slovakia, the applicants, Mr. A. Bystrý and Mr. M. Bystrý, were described in the judgment as coming from a Roma settlement, indicating their Roma background. The case concerned the vulnerability of individuals from a Roma community to police violence and the lack of an effective investigation into their allegations of ill-treatment. On 12 April 2020, during a police intervention in Slovakia, both applicants were arrested. The second applicant, Mr. M. Bystrý, was struck on the head with a metal baton, resulting in a depressed fracture of the frontal bone and multiple contusions, with an expected healing period of about thirty days. The first applicant, Mr. A. Bystrý, suffered concussion, contusions, and abrasions after being dragged to a police car while handcuffed, with injuries requiring five to six days to heal. Despite claims by the authorities that the force used was justified by the applicants’ conduct, the European Court of Human Rights found that the injuries were sufficiently serious to meet the threshold of Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court held that the force used was disproportionate and not strictly necessary, and that the subsequent investigation was inadequate, relying too heavily on police accounts and failing to thoroughly examine all evidence. The Court found violations of Article 3 in both its substantive and procedural aspects, awarding the applicants a total of EUR 16,500 in non-pecuniary damages and EUR 6,410 for costs and expenses.
